en: Jātaka:
Miscellaneous Section,
Chapter on the Rice Field of Śāli Rice.
5. The Bhisajātaka:
“Horses, cattle, silver, gold, and a pleasing wife—may he obtain these here.”
"May he who took away your lotus roots, O brahmin, be united with sons and wives!
May he [wear] garlands and Kāśī sandalwood!"
"May you have many sons, may they prosper;
maintain a fierce longing for sensual pleasures,
O Brahmin, you who took away my lotus roots."
“Abounding in grain, successful in his farming,
with sons at home, wealthy, and possessing all desires—
one who dwells at home should not perceive decline.”
O Brahmin, he who gave you these medicinal herbs—
let that Kshatriya be one who acts with resolute strength,
a king of kings, powerful and renowned.
May he who stole your lotus roots,
O Brahmin, rule over the earth bounded by the four oceans;
may that Brahmin remain one who is not free from passion.
The illustrious lord of the realm, who is devoted to the paths of the moments and constellations,
should honor him, O Brahmin, who gave you those lotus roots.
Let the whole world consider him a reciter who has mastered all the Vedas on every side;
let the people of the countryside, having approached him, honor him as an ascetic.
O Brahmin, he who took away your medicinal herbs shall enjoy a prosperous,
excellent village with four gates,
for it has been granted to him by Vāsava.
May he who took away your lotus roots, O Brahmin, meet his death without having overcome his passions;
may he become a village headman in the midst of his companions.
Delighting in dances and songs,
that king did not suffer any misfortune whatsoever,
O Brahmin, as for those lotus roots which you took away.
May she who was appointed by a single king, having conquered the earth,
as the foremost among a thousand women—
may she become the most excellent among those with parted hair.
O Brahmin, those medicinal herbs which you have brought—
let her eat them with confidence, for they are fit for all the seers gathered together, being delicious to consume.
Let her go away boasting of her gain,
O Brahmin— she who took away your lotus roots.
Let her be a resident of the Great Monastery.
Let him be a builder of new works in Gajaṅgalā;
let him provide light and openings by day— he,
O Brahmin, who took away your lotus roots.
Let him be bound with six hundred snares;
let him depart from the lovely forests to the royal capital;
let him be slain by all those who cook him.
O Brahmin, he who threw those medicinal herbs at you—
wearing a garland of red lac, with his ears pierced by small ear-rings,
and struck by a staff— he has entered the mouth of a serpent.
"Let him who stole your lotus roots,
O Brahmin, wander with his head shorn and bound by a rope.
"He who says that what is not lost is lost," [said the other].
"Whether one obtains and enjoys sensual pleasures,
or whether one encounters death in the midst of the household life,
or whether one fears anything at all, O sirs— "
“Whatever they seek while wandering the world—
whatever is desirable, lovely, dear,
and pleasing to many here in this world of the living— ”
"Why do the seers not praise sensual pleasures?
"Indeed, in sensual pleasures they are slain and bound;
in sensual pleasures suffering and fear are born."
Negligent and intoxicated by sensual pleasures,
they commit evil deeds out of delusion.
Having produced evil through their wicked nature, they...
Upon the breakup of the body, they go to hell;
having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure,
for that reason the seers do not praise sensual pleasures.
“Investigating the matter,
I took the lotus roots from the bank and placed them on dry land;
the seers dwell there pure and free from evil.”
"These are your medicinal roots, O student of the holy life.
"They are not actors, nor are they for amusement;
they are not kinsmen, nor are they companions."
“O Thousand-Eyed One, upon what support do you sport with the seers, O King of Gods?
“You are my teacher and my father.”
This is indeed the support for one who has stumbled, O Brahmā:
forgive this single transgression, O you of vast wisdom;
for the wise do not become slaves to anger.
“May all these worthy ones be well-disposed toward this fragrant offering for a single night, which we,
as lords of beings, have seen bestowed upon the seers.”
“Whatever lotus roots the brahmin has accepted— myself, Sāriputta,
Moggallāna, and Kassapa;”
Anuruddha, Puṇṇa, and Ānanda—
these were the seven brothers at that time;
and Uppalavaṇṇā was their sister.
At that time, Khujjuttarā was a female slave;
Cittagahapati was a slave;
and Sātāgira was a yakkha.
At that time, the elephant was Pālileyya,
the excellent monkey Madhudā,
and Kāḷudāyī was Sakka.
“Thus you should remember this as a Jātaka.
The fifth is the Bhisajātakam.
